items.title: Biography
items.short_bio: Bay Fujimoto is a designer and researcher based in Houston, Texas. He studied architecture at Rice University and works at Low Design Office.
items.long_bio:
His practice sits at the intersection of design, technology, and material culture. Trained as an architect, he is drawn to the conditions under which objects, spaces, and systems acquire meaning through use rather than through intent — the scuff on a handrail, the shortcut worn into a lawn, the form that outlasts its original purpose.

At Rice University he studied the formal and cultural logic of buildings as objects, and the ways institutions shape the people who move through them. He completed a semester abroad through the Rice School of Architecture Paris program, where he began thinking more seriously about the relationship between archival practices and design research.

At Low Design Office he works on projects that take their constraints seriously — material, budgetary, organizational — and finds in those constraints the conditions for something honest. He is interested in work that resists the reduction of design to styling or to the management of appearances.

This site is an attempt to document that work in a form closer to an archive than a portfolio: less argument, more evidence.

items.title: Biography
items.short_bio: Bay Fujimoto is a designer and architecture student based in Houston, Texas. He is completing a Bachelor of Architecture at Rice University.
items.long_bio:
His work sits at the intersection of architectural history, design research, and material culture. He is interested in how buildings and objects are used, accumulated, and remembered — the ways in which ordinary things carry traces of the lives they have been part of.

At Rice University he has studied the formal logic of buildings as objects, the history of modernism's institutional forms, and the relationship between design and everyday life. A semester abroad in Paris through the Rice School of Architecture deepened his interest in archival research as a design method.

Alongside academic work he has taken on design and research projects across professional and independent contexts. He is drawn to work that is specific rather than universal, that takes the particular conditions of a problem seriously rather than defaulting to generic solutions.

This site is an ongoing attempt to keep a record of that work — not as a portfolio, but as an archive.

items.title: Wencun Village
items.thesis: Set in the village of Wencun, China, this calligraphy library and workshop bridges past and present through hybrid construction approach. The building is rooted in traditional brickwork techniques, but integrates contemporary technologies to enhance ventilation and lighting.

subitems.caption: Inspired by Professor Wang Shu’s daily calligraphy practice, I generated hundreds of hand-drawn, imaginary characters, letting gesture and repetition guide form. These marks, though unreadable, became a generative language for the architecture itself to influence proportions, rhythms, and porosity.
The form became rationalized over time to carve out larger spaces and to simplify circulation.
A 1:4 scale model, designed parametrically, tested brick’s capability to create double curvature forms. Over 600 bricks were cast to create the model.
Oblique plan drawing reveals the linear layout of program.

Unrolled elevations illustrate the textural effects of rotated brickwork. The brick walls are parametrically designed, with rotated and offset units that create a porous surface for natural ventilation and different lighting conditions based on the program.
The building sits on an existing pond that irrigates the nearby rice paddy.
The architecture embraces slowness and tactility: its thick walls, deep eaves, and hand-laid bonds speak to a collective memory of making.
